summary: Reports on how fast the MD5 message digest algorithm can be implemented in software and hardware, and asks whether it can keep up with the IP bandwidth available at the time. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1810 is a speed test for MD5, the fingerprint algorithm IPv6 proposed to use for checking packets. It measures how fast MD5 runs on real computers, works out why it cannot go faster, and suggests a change that would let it keep up with fast networks.

questions: can md5 keep up with network bandwidth
how does md5 parallel chaining work
subtitle: Measuring how fast MD5 can authenticate data in hardware and software, and what to do about it.

tldr.problem: MD5 had been proposed as a default authentication mechanism for IPv6, but it had to be shown that it could keep up with the IP bandwidth available at the time.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC measures MD5 on eight platforms in software and works out what the algorithm's structure allows in hardware, finding that its block chaining limits how much of the work can run at the same time.
tldr.outcome: The best software rate measured was 87 Mbps and hardware tops out at 256 Mbps, below the 100 Mbps TCP and 130 Mbps UDP over ATM rates of the day. The RFC proposes a 16-way parallel chaining of MD5 and asks that alternatives be considered.

today: RFC 1810 is an Informational memo, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It measures MD5 as it stood in June 1995 and proposes a change to the algorithm; it defines no protocol.

sections.title: Why the Speed Matters
sections.content:
MD5 is an authentication algorithm that has been proposed as one authentication option in IPv6. RFC 1321 describes the MD5 algorithm and gives a reference implementation. When enabled, the MD5 algorithm operates over the entire data packet, including the header, with dummy values for the volatile fields.

The RFC addresses how fast MD5 can be implemented in software and hardware, and whether it supports the currently available IP bandwidth. It frames the question as the general issue of checksumming and security at high speed in IPv6. IPv6 has no header checksum, which IPv4 has, but proposes an authentication digest over the entire body of the packet, including the header where volatile fields are zeroed. The performance of that mechanism is what the report examines.
sections.plainLanguage: If a security check on incoming packets takes longer than the packets arrive, the router cannot keep up with the data. This report asks whether MD5 would cause that.

sections.title: Measured Performance
sections.content:
The code measured was an optimized version of the MD5 reference implementation from RFC 1321, and the results come from the performance test md5 -t, modified to prohibit on-chip caching of the data block. The measured rates were 87 Mbps on a DEC Alpha at 190 MHz, 33 Mbps on an HP 9000/720, 48 Mbps on an IBM RS/6000 7006 with a PPC 601 at 80 MHz, 31 Mbps on an Intel i486/66 running NetBSD, 44 Mbps on an Intel Pentium/90 running NeXTStep, 52 Mbps on an SGI IP-20 running IRIX 5.2, 37 Mbps on a Sun SPARC-10/51 and SPARC-20/50 running SunOS 4.1.3, and 57 Mbps on a Sun SPARC-20/71 running SunOS 4.1.3.

The report says these rates do not keep up with the currently available IP bandwidth, for example 100 Mbps TCP and 130 Mbps UDP over a Fore SBA-200 ATM host interface in a Sun SPARC-20/71. It also notes that values as high as 100 Mbps have been reported for the DEC Alpha, but that those reflect on-chip caching of the data, and that it is not clear whether in-memory off-chip cache or on-chip cache performance measures are more relevant to IP performance.
sections.plainLanguage: Testing shows MD5 running between 31 and 87 million bits per second on the fastest computers of the time, while the networks around them were already carrying 100 to 130 million bits per second.

sections.title: Why MD5 Cannot Go Faster
sections.content:
The MD5 algorithm is a block-chained hashing algorithm. The first block is hashed with an initial seed, and the resulting hash is summed with the seed to become the seed for the next block. When the last block is computed, its next-seed value becomes the hash for the whole stream. The seed for a block therefore depends on both the hash and the seed of the block before it, and as a result blocks cannot be hashed in parallel.

Each 16-word, that is 64-byte, block is hashed in 64 basic steps using a 4-word intermediate hash, which is collapsed at the end, and the 64 steps are 16 groups of 4 steps, one step per intermediate hash word. Each step is composed of two table lookups, one rotation, a 3-component logical operation and 4 additions. The best parallelisation possible leaves the logical function to the last step, and the resulting tree shows that sequences of the binary operation tree cannot be overlapped while the optimised hardware tree can, by one time step. The binary tree takes 5 time units per step of the algorithm and permits at best 3-way parallelism, which in software means 20 instructions per word of input.

From this the report derives two software rates. A computer capable of M MIPS can support a data bandwidth of M/20 * 32 Mbps, that is 1.6 times its MIPS rate, so a 100 MIPS machine can support a 160 Mbps stream, provided register reads and writes overlap entirely with computation. Without any parallelism there are 8 operations per step and 4 steps per word, so 32 operations per word and the data rate equals the MIPS rate. Measured results on eight machines are compared against predictions made from SpecInt92 numbers as MIPS estimators.

The hardware rate takes 3 time units per step, that is 12 time units per word of input. Hardware that can do an operation such as a 32-bit addition in N nanoseconds supports a data bandwidth of 32/12/N bits per second. For CMOS, an operation including register retrieval and storage costs about 5.2 ns, and with 6 clocks through the most highly parallelised implementation that gives 31.2 ns per 32-bit word, or 256 Mbps. The report notes that this will not keep pace with existing hardware, which is capable of link speeds in excess of 622 Mbps for ATM. By comparison, IPv4 uses the Internet checksum, which can be performed in 32-bit-wide units in excess of 1 Gbps in an existing low-cost PLD, and can also be parallelised by computing partial sums and reducing the result.
sections.plainLanguage: MD5 works step by step in a chain where each step must wait for the previous one to finish, so the blocks of a packet cannot be hashed at the same time. That is the reason it cannot be sped up much.

sections.title: The Proposed Modification
sections.content:
The report considers two ways to raise the performance of the IPv6 authentication mechanism: increasing the hardware performance of MD5 by slightly modifying the algorithm, or proposing a replacement algorithm. It discusses the modification briefly, and notes that alternate algorithms capable of 3.5 times the speed of MD5 have been discussed elsewhere.

MD5 uses block chaining to ensure sensitivity to block order, and block chaining also prevents arbitrary parallelism, which can be as much a benefit to a spoofer as to the user. MD5 can be slightly altered so that a predetermined finite number of blocks are processed from independent seeds, such that the I-th block is part of the I mod K-th chain. The resulting K digests themselves form a message, which can be MD5-encoded using a single-block algorithm. The report says this idea was proposed independently by the author and by Burt Kaliski of RSA.

The goal is to support finite parallelism, to provide adequate bandwidth at current processing rates, without providing arbitrary power for spoofing. The report says it would require further analysis to ensure an adequate level of security. For current technology and network bandwidth, a minimum of 4-way parallel chaining would suffice and 16-way chaining would be preferable, which would support network bandwidth of 1 Gbps with 4-way chaining in CMOS hardware. The chaining parallelism should be a multiple of 4-way, to generate a complete block of digests, since there are 4 words per digest and 16 words per block.
sections.plainLanguage: Split the data into a fixed number of chains and hash them side by side instead of one after another. Sixteen chains would let existing hardware handle a gigabit per second.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The whole document addresses a mechanism for providing security in IPv6, and MD5 is the proposed default optional authentication mechanism for IPv6 traffic. The report says its concern is that security mechanisms such as MD5 that cannot support high bandwidth with available hardware will compromise their deployment, and ultimately the security of the systems they are meant to maintain.

The IPv6 requirements document emphasises that IPv6 implementations should not compromise performance compared to IPv4, presumably despite IPv6's increased functionality, and that required optional components of IPv6 should be held to the same standard. The report says MD5 compromises performance, and so its use as a required default option in IPv6 should be reconsidered. Using MD5 as the default for the required authentication option may compromise security in high-bandwidth systems, because enabling the option causes performance degradation, which defeats its inclusion as an IPv6 option, and as a result the authentication option may be disabled entirely.

It concludes that it is important for the use of authentication in high-performance systems that an alternative mechanism be available in IPv6 from the outset. This may require the specification of multiple required authentication algorithms, one slower but believed strong, and one faster but inspiring somewhat less confidence. The conclusions repeat the numbers: MD5 cannot be implemented in existing technology at rates in excess of 256 Mbps in hardware, or 86 Mbps in software, so it cannot be used to support IP authentication in existing networks at existing rates, and although MD5 will support higher bandwidth in the future through technological advances, those will be offset by similar advances in networking.
sections.plainLanguage: The report's conclusion is that making a slow security check part of every packet may make people turn it off altogether, which is worse than having nothing. It asks for a faster alternative to be available from the start.
